oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and its Leap into Diabetes Management
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Artificial intelligence (AI) has transitioned from theoretical explorations to a transformative force driving innovation across multiple industries. Generative AI, a specialized subset, showcases exceptional capabilities in generating content, such as text, images, and music, and solving complex problems. In health care, AI is revolutionizing diabetes management by enabling continuous glucose monitoring, personalized treatment plans, and affordable insulin delivery solutions. These advancements are particularly significant for resource-limited settings like India, where cost-effective, scalable, and accessible solutions are critical. From AI-driven predictive algorithms to the development of affordable three-dimensional-printed insulin pumps, the technology is democratizing healthcare innovation. Despite these benefits, challenges persist in addressing fears related to job displacement, data privacy, and misuse. Furthermore, legal barriers surrounding accountability, intellectual property, and compliance with data protection laws require immediate attention. This paper explores the transformative potential of AI in healthcare, emphasizing its role in diabetes management while highlighting the ethical, legal, and social considerations essential for its responsible integration.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Comparison of Two Short-acting Insulin Formulations in the Management of Blood Glucose in Undergoing Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery Patients
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Background: Postoperative high blood glucose levels can affect the prognosis following coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). Although actrapid and fast-acting insulin aspart (FIASP) are approved for intravenous (IV) use, very limited data on their safety and efficacy in patients undergoing cardiac procedures are available. This study compared the efficacy of IV actrapid and FIASP in maintaining blood glucose levels in patients with diabetes undergoing CABG. Methods: In this retrospective, single-center study, people with diabetes who underwent CABG surgery were included in the study. Data on patients undergoing CABG surgery who received injection actrapid or FIASP perioperatively were collected to control blood glucose. The target blood glucose level was 150–180 mg/dl, and the sliding scale therapy was followed to maintain the glucose levels within this range. Blood glucose level <70 mg/dl was considered hypoglycemia. Data were collected at baseline (day 0) and on days 2 and 6 after the surgery. Results: The study included 100 patients, 50 in each of the FIASP-treated group and the actrapid-treated group. Fasting and mean blood glucose levels significantly decreased in both FIASP and actrapid groups from day 2 to day 6 after surgery. The total dose of insulin required daily was significantly lower in the FIASP group despite the high inotropic levels at baseline. There was no statistically significant difference in the fasting and mean blood glucose levels between the FIASP and actrapid groups. Conclusion: FIASP and actrapid safely and effectively control the blood glucose levels post CABG; however, the units required for FIASP were less than those required for actrapid, and patients in the FIASP group require minimal insulin at discharge.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Safety and Efficacy of Semaglutide in Type 2 Diabetes Patients: A Real-World Study
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Background: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is considered a prevalent condition in India, with 8% of the population affected and an additional 25 million classified as prediabetic. Recent advancements in treatment strategies for T2DM include using glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide. This study aims to evaluate the effects of semaglutide on glycemic control, weight management, lipid profiles, renal function, and liver enzymes in these patients. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study analyzed data from 100 T2DM patients treated with semaglutide for 9 months. Patients were initially administered 3 mg of semaglutide, and later dose was titrated to either 7 mg or 14 mg in subsequent visits. Baseline and follow-up data on glycemic control, weight, lipid profiles, renal function, and liver enzymes were analyzed. Statistical analyses were conducted using Microsoft Excel and SPSS, with P < 0.05 considered statistically significant. Results: Semaglutide treatment significantly reduced fasting blood glucose and hemoglobin A1c levels (P < 0.001). A significant decrease in weight and body mass index was noted over the study period (P < 0.0001). Improvements were observed in liver enzyme levels, with significant decreases in serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase and serum glutamic-pyruvic transaminase (P < 0.0001), lipid profile including reductions in total cholesterol, triglycerides (TGs), and low-density lipoprotein, and an increase in high-density lipoprotein (P < 0.017). Liver FibroScan markers like controlled attenuation parameter and E (kPa) were also reduced significantly (P < 0.0001). Renal function markers also improved significantly (P < 0.0001). Conclusions: Semaglutide significantly improved glycemic control, reduced body weight, and lipid and renal profiles in T2DM patients. These findings support the use of semaglutide as an effective treatment option for managing T2DM, demonstrating its beneficial impact on multiple aspects of metabolic health.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Screening of Indian Patients with Diabetes for Detection of Microalbuminuria using Dipstick Test: A Retrospective Observational Study
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Context: Microalbuminuria (MAU) is an early indicator of kidney damage in uncontrolled diabetes linked with elevated cardiovascular and renal risks. Aims: This study aims to determine the prevalence of MAU and identify clinical predictors in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) patients. Settings and Design: A retrospective, multicenter analysis of clinical records from 2600 diabetes centers across India, conducted during the “World Diabetes Day” campaign (November 14–30, 2022). Materials and Methods: Clinical records of 63,570 T2DM patients screened using Micral® test for MAU were analyzed. Data on demographics, comorbidities, and clinical parameters were collected. Statistical Analysis Used: The statistical analyses were conducted using R Studio Version 2022.07.2. Results: MAU prevalence was 36.9% (n = 17,275). The mean age of patients was 54.8 ± 11.9 years, with 64% being male. Key predictors included hemoglobin A1c (odds ratio [OR] = 1.18, P < 0.001), diabetes duration (OR = 1.04, P < 0.001), hypertension duration (OR = 1.03, P < 0.001), and diastolic BP (OR = 1.01, P < 0.001). Males had slightly lower odds of MAU compared to females (OR = 0.96, P = 0.198). Conclusions: Four out of ten patients with type 2 diabetes suffered from MAU in our study. Therefore, it is strongly recommended to screen every diabetes patient in clinical practice to detect early signs of kidney damage.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Do-It-yourself Artificial Pancreas Systems: User Perspectives, Glycemic Control, and Quality of Life in Type 1 Diabetes
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Introduction and Objective: The emergence of open-source automated insulin delivery (AID) systems, often developed and supported by patient communities, has introduced a transformative approach to diabetes management. These systems integrate continuous glucose monitoring (CGM), insulin pumps, and algorithm-driven smartphone applications to automate insulin delivery. This study aimed to explore the usage patterns, glycemic outcomes, and user perceptions of DIY AID systems (DIYAPS), specifically focusing on their effectiveness and impact on quality of life (QOL) in individuals with type 1 diabetes (T1D). Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted using a structured questionnaire distributed among members of the Loopers Community WhatsApp group from May to August 2024. The survey collected data on demographics, computer literacy, DIYAPS components, duration of use, CGM metrics before and after adoption, and user feedback on system usability. One of the coauthors, who is a DIYAPS user, also contributed a detailed user perspective, providing firsthand insights to enrich the study findings. Responses were anonymized, and ethical research protocols were adhered to throughout the study. Results: A total of 10 participants (50% male, 50% female) from different parts of the country completed the survey. The average time in range improved significantly from 63% ±10% to 80% ±12%, while time above range and time below range decreased from 28% ±12% to 17% ±14% and 13% ±11% to 7% ±6%, respectively. Mean hemoglobin A1C levels dropped from 8.02% to 6.75%. Participants reported reduced fear of hypoglycemia, better sleep quality, and greater flexibility in daily routines. The coauthor’s user perspective highlighted additional benefits, such as improved overnight glycemic control and reduced dependence on manual adjustments, alongside practical challenges like device maintenance. Conclusion: DIYAPS demonstrates significant potential in improving glycemic control and enhancing QOL for individuals with T1D. Despite technical challenges, the systems provide a cost-effective and customizable alternative to commercial AID options. The findings support further integration of open-source AID systems into clinical practice while advocating for collaborative care and longitudinal studies to assess long-term outcomes and safety.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Association of Elevated C-reactive Protein with Body Mass Index and Gender in Individuals with Diabetes: A Cross-sectional Analysis
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Background: Numerous factors have been determined to impact the levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) synthesized by the hepatocytes. When an infectious or inflammatory condition is in its acute stage, the level rises. Existing evidence observed elevated levels of CRP in diabetes, but data on the impact of various parameters on CRP levels in people with diabetes are still lacks. Aim: The cross-sectional study aims to investigate the association between CRP levels and body mass index (BMI), gender, hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), and other clinical indicators in individuals with type 2 diabetes. Methods: The study was conducted at a comprehensive diabetes care center in Kerala, India, and included 1006 individuals with type 2 diabetes with a median age of 63 years. The association between CRP levels and various parameters was analyzed using statistical methods. Results: The findings from the study demonstrate a strong correlation between BMI and CRP levels. There were notable differences in CRP levels between the BMI groups of normal, overweight, and obese individuals. The intriguing finding was that women were reported to have higher CRP levels compared to males. The findings of the subgroup analysis, depending on the duration of diabetes, showed that BMI, HbA1c, and age had distinct impacts on CRP levels. While GLPs and gliflozins had no effect on CRP levels, statin use dramatically reduces CRP levels, according to analysis of the effects of several drugs on CRP levels. Conclusion: The study eventually reached the conclusion that to prevent adversities, it is critical to evaluate body responses, such as inflammation and the proteins associated with it, because diabetes is a lifestyle disorder that can have devastating implications.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Disability, distress and delayed access to care in functional neurological disorder: cross-sectional study from an Australian tertiary clinic
oai_dc:dc.dc:description:
Background Functional neurological disorder (FND) is a common condition, but there remain substantial gaps in our understanding of its effects, particularly on severity of disability and health status.
Aims To characterise disability, quality of life and psychological and somatic symptom comorbidity in individuals with FND attending a specialist multidisciplinary clinic in Australia.
Method We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of patients assessed at an FND clinic in Sydney, Australia, between August 2022 and February 2025. We assessed disability (World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS 2.0)), health-related quality of life (EQ-5D five-level version (EQ-5D-5L), 36-Item Short Form Health Survey), psychological distress (Depression Anxiety and Stress Scale-21, Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K10)) and somatic symptom severity (Patient Health Questionnaire-15 (PHQ-15)).
Results The cohort (N = 105) was predominantly female (74.3%), with a mean age of 35.4 (s.d. = 13.3) years. Functional seizures (46.7%) and functional weakness (45.7%) were the most common presentations. Only 33.7% were employed; 42.9% were unable to work because of FND. The average delay from diagnosis to clinic assessment was 356 days (s.d. = 463). WHODAS 2.0 scores indicated high levels of disability, exceeding international norms for both physical and mental illness. EQ-5D-5L scores were low, with 15.8% reporting a health state rated as ‘worse than death’. Psychological distress and somatic symptom severity were high: 49.5% scored in the K10 ‘very high’ range and 54.5% had high PHQ-15 scores.
Conclusions FND is associated with significant functional disability, poor quality of life and high levels of psychological and somatic symptom comorbidity. Delays in accessing appropriate care and high rates of vocational disruption highlight the need for earlier diagnosis and better access to integrated, multidisciplinary FND services in Australia.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Evaluation of clinicopathological features of renal biopsies in non-lupus rheumatic diseases: a university hospital experience
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Renal involvement is a common condition in rheumatologic diseases. The aim of this study was to evaluate the clinical presentations and histopathological results in patients diagnosed with non-lupus rheumatic diseases who underwent renal biopsy. The records of 900 renal biopsies performed at our hospital between 2004 and 2023 were retrospectively reviewed, and 139 patients diagnosed with non-lupus rheumatic diseases were included. Data on demographic and clinical characteristics, laboratory results, renal biopsy indications, and histopathological findings were obtained from hospital records. Among the patients, 46 had rheumatoid arthritis (RA), 31 had ankylosing spondylitis (AS), 31 had familial Mediterranean fever (FMF), 17 had Behçet’s disease (BD), and 14 had psoriasis (PsO). The most common indication for biopsy was hematuria + subnephrotic proteinuria, accounting for 17.3%. The most frequent pathological diagnosis was amyloidosis (36.7%), followed by focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) (19.4%), chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) (8.6%), immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy (7.9%), and membranous glomerulonephritis (7.2%). A significant difference was noted among rheumatologic diseases groups according to the reasons for biopsy (p = 0.031) and pathological diagnoses (p = 0.003). The frequency of amyloidosis was higher in the FMF group with 61.3%, FSGS was higher in the BD group with 47.1%, and IGA nephropathy was higher in the PsO group with 35.7%. The characteristics of renal involvement in rheumatic diseases differ depending on the underlying disease. Close monitoring of renal functions and performing biopsy when necessary are critically important in these patients.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Comparative Pain Score (Numeric Rating Scale-II) Analysis of Pre-existing and a Newly Introduced 4 mm Pen Needles in Indian Population with Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Background: For the majority of people with diabetes, one of the main reasons for denying or delaying insulin therapy is an extreme fear of pain during insulin injections. However, in this digital era, quantum leaps in needle technologies open novel avenues for painless injections. Aim: The longitudinal observational study, conducted in a comprehensive diabetes care center in Kerala, India, evaluates the effectiveness of a recently introduced 4 mm needle and 4 mm needles hitherto in India to reduce pain during insulin injection in people with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) and T2DM using the numeric rating scale (NRS-II) pain score. Results: The statistical analyses revealed that the newly introduced 4 mm needle significantly reduced pain in the cohort with type 2 diabetes compared to the existing 4 mm needles routinely used by the cohort. Regarding the cohort with type 1 diabetes, even though the use of the newly introduced needle reduced pain while taking injections, the NRS-II pain score was not statistically significant, which may be due to the small sample size, noncompliance to advanced needle technologies. The study also analyzes the influence of demographic factors on the pain score. Conclusion: In the wholesome attempt, the study urges using advanced needle technologies for painless insulin injections and improved diabetes management.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Diabetes Status among Adults in Rural India: Rural Noncommunicable Disease Clinic Observation
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Backround: Diabetes mellitus represents a widespread global health trouble. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are responsible for 60% of all fatalities in India, with diabetes representing 3% of these cases. India has launched the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Disease (NP-NCD) under the framework of the National Health Mission (NHM). Aim: This study was undertaken to see the number of people over 30 years old with more than 200mg/dl random blood sugar level. Methodology: The methodology employed in this study focused on evaluating diabetic levels in adults residing in a small region of rural Newai, Rajasthan, India, through a quantitative lens. A descriptive study was carried out in Newai, Rajasthan, India, to evaluate diabetic levels among adults during non-communicable disease clinics.A total of 67 adults aged over 30 years were included, with 62 samples available for analysis. The investigation employed socio-demographic data alongside a blood sugar assessment instrument utilizing the Dr. Morepen BG-03 Gluco One Glucometer. The analysis employed descriptive statistics, adhering to a significance threshold of P <0.05. Ethical considerations encompassed obtaining written permission, ensuring informed consent, maintaining confidentiality, and providing health education for the entire sample. The study was conducted during a training clinic focused on non-communicable diseases for community health officers. Result: A total of 62 individuals were involved, with an average age of 54.5 years. According to the investigation, 2% of participants had random blood sugar levels above 200 mg/dl, whereas 98% of individuals had random blood sugar levels below 200 mg/dl. The average blood sugar level, calculated at a 95% confidence interval, was 112.0806 ±6.186 (110.54-113.62).The entire sample received health education, encompassing individuals at risk of developing diabetes. Conclusion: this study found that random blood sugar levels exceeding 200mg/dl are infrequent in the rural Newai area of Rajasthan, India, suggesting a low risk of diabetes among adults over 30 years of age.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Understanding the Preference of a Dipeptidyl Peptidase-4 Inhibitor and its Combination Therapy in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus among Indian Clinicians
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Background: Multiple dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP4is) are available in India. The class of DPP4i presents as a heterogeneous group with differences among the molecules. Thus, there is a need to evaluate the choice of DPP4i and its combinations among Indian clinicians. This survey aims to assess the choice of DPP4i and its combinations among Indian clinicians in the management of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Methodology: This was a cross-sectional questionnaire-based survey of clinicians in India conducted between December 2022 and March 2023. Data were analyzed and expressed using descriptive statistics. Results: Among the 1033 clinicians in the survey, the majority (71.73%) were in the age group of 31–50 years, 66.6% had a postgraduate degree in medicine, and 74.93% had a private consulting practice. Almost half of the participants opined that the response of DPP4i is similar in T2DM patients irrespective of age (47.24%) and body mass index (46.95%). Among the various DPP4i available in India, sitagliptin was opined to provide greater glycated hemoglobin reduction (72.80%), faster reduction in blood glucose (71.25%), and greater improvement in glycemic variability (73.28%) by the majority of the clinicians. Most clinicians opined sitagliptin as the preferred DPP4i in T2DM patients irrespective of age and in various comorbidities. Around 65.25% of clinicians opined that sitagliptin was associated with fewer adverse events in patients with T2DM. In terms of combination therapy, the majority of the clinicians opined sitagliptin/dapagliflozin was most preferred in T2DM patients (81.51%: In T2DM with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, 79.28%: In T2DM with heart failure, 53.63%: In T2DM with chronic kidney disease) among the various DPP4i/sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) available in India. Conclusions: The survey conducted among over 1000 clinicians across India is suggestive of sitagliptin and sitagliptin/dapagliflozin being the preferred DPP4i and DPP4i/SGLT2i, respectively, among Indian clinicians for the management of a wide range of patients with T2DM.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Real-world Use of Oral Semaglutide in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes in India: A Retrospective Study
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Background: Oral semaglutide has shown efficacy in clinical trials worldwide; however, real-world evidence in Indian settings is scarce. The current study examined the effectiveness of oral semaglutide in patients with type 2 diabetes within the context of routine clinical practice in Indian settings. Methodology: This retrospective, multicenter, observational study assessed the effectiveness of oral semaglutide in adult patients with type 2 diabetes who had inadequate glycemic control (HbA1c ≥6.5). The included patients need to have ≥1 HbA1c report within 12 weeks of the study initiation. The primary end point was change in HbA1c% from baseline to end of study (EOS; 30 weeks), with secondary end points including changes in body weight, waist circumference, and body mass index (BMI). These end points were evaluated for patients who were on oral semaglutide at EOS. Results: Of 414 screened patients, 340 were included in the study, with 176 patients on oral semaglutide at EOS. A mean reduction of 0.96 ± 1.02% (P < 0.001) in HbA1c from baseline to EOS was observed, with greater reductions in patients with 5–10 years of diabetes. At EOS, 92.6% of patients achieved a target of ≥1% HbA1c reduction from baseline. In addition, significant reductions in body weight (6.04 ± 5.40 kg, P < 0.001), waist circumference (3.47 ± 5.42 cm, P < 0.001), and BMI (1.94 ± 1.42 kg/m2, P < 0.001) were observed at EOS. Conclusion: Oral semaglutide shows promise as a therapeutic option for glycemic control and weight management in diabetic patients in Indian settings. However, further randomized clinical trials in Indian patients are warranted to validate these findings and optimize further treatment strategies.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Comparative Evaluation of the Precision and Accuracy of Five Available Glucometers in India
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Background: The monitoring of glucose plays an inevitable role in diabetes management. Over the years, technological leaps in diabetes management have contributed immensely to improving the quality of life of people with diabetes. Along with the multitude of benefits, these technologies provide, particularly glucose meters, the chances of compromises in the accuracy and precision of these devices also exist due to high competition among the manufacturers. Hence, it is essential, that both people with diabetes and healthcare professionals be aware of the accuracy and precision of glucose meters and whether they meet the accuracy standards recommended by international organizations such as the International Organization for Standardization and the Food and Drug Administration to avoid severe consequences. Aim: The study aims to evaluate and compare the accuracy, performance, and precision of five glucosemeters On Call Plus, Cool, One Touch, Contour Plus, and Accu-chek Instant in people without diabetes, with type1 diabetes, and with type 2 diabetes. Result: The results revealed that all the glucose meters chosen for the study showed reasonably satisfactory clinical accuracy and precision in people without and with type 2 diabetes. However, in the cohort with type 1 diabetes, the performance of the meters was only moderately satisfactory. Conclusion: The study brings into the limelight the importance of evaluating the accuracy and precision of glucose monitoring devices, irrespective of blindly believing the technology.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Common Prescription Errors in Diabetes: Physician’s Perspective
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Background: Managing diabetes requires precise medication regimens, particularly with insulin and oral hypoglycemic agents (OHAs). However, prescription errors are prevalent in diabetes care and pose significant risks to patient safety, potentially resulting in severe acute and chronic complications. Despite the preventable nature of these errors, they persist in clinical practice, underscoring the need for improved prescribing practices and multidisciplinary care. Objective: This study aims to identify common prescription errors and faults in diabetes care, based on the perspectives of physicians, to propose strategies for reducing such errors and enhancing patient safety. Methodology: A qualitative research approach was adopted, involving semistructured interviews with 20 physicians at a comprehensive diabetes center in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala. Participants, with over 20 years of clinical experience in diabetes care, shared their observations on prescription errors. The data were analyzed thematically using R software, and ethical guidelines were followed, including informed consent and confidentiality assurances. Results: Key themes identified include basic prescription practices, where OHAs were frequently prescribed, with insulin often reserved as a last-resort therapy, and GLP-1 analogs rarely prescribed. Prescription legibility issues were common, with illegible handwritten prescriptions lacking critical details. Prescribing issues such as overprescribing, misprescribing, and underprescribing were widely reported. Contraindications were frequently overlooked, with inappropriate prescriptions for patients with renal failure, older adults, and those with liver impairment. Incorrect dosing of insulin and metformin was identified due to inadequate adjustments or cumulative overdosing. Drug–drug interactions, including between GLP-1 analogs and DPP-4 inhibitors, and thiazide diuretics with sodium-glucose transport protein 2 inhibitors, were noted. Transitional prescription errors during care transitions were also highlighted, often linked to poor communication and discrepancies in medication lists. Conclusion: The study highlights critical challenges in diabetes prescription practices and emphasizes the need for personalized care plans, regular medication reviews, and technological integration to reduce errors and improve patient outcomes. Continuous medical education and adherence to evidence-based guidelines are essential for advancing safe and effective diabetes management.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: A Snapshot of Glycemic Response to Food Using a Continuous Glucose Monitor
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Understanding how specific foods affect one’s blood glucose levels can help diabetic patients make better meal choices. A 35-year-old male diabetic patient was monitored for 6 months using a continuous glucose monitor (CGM). The obtained glycemic response curves for various types of food were analyzed. Meal composition played a crucial role in determining the glucose spike. Foods with high carbohydrate content increased sugars much higher than foods with balanced macronutrients. Combining protein and fat-rich foods with high-carbohydrate foods lowered the sugar spikes caused by a pure carbohydrate meal. Fruits, due to their high fiber and water content, although loaded with carbohydrates, did not spike the sugars much. Commercially available diabetic nutrition powders also had a good glycemic profile. Thus, CGM plays a crucial role in improving the health outcomes of people with diabetes by allowing them to choose the right quantity and quality of food to eat.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: A Randomized, Placebo-controlled Study to Assess the Efficacy and Safety of Herbal Extract and Micronutrient Blend Supplementation in People with Prediabetes
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Background and Objective: Prediabetes is a precursor stage to type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), characterized by elevated blood glucose levels. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of herbal extract and micronutrient blend supplementation in managing prediabetes. Materials and Methods: This multicentric, randomized, placebo-controlled study involved 319 subjects with prediabetes (159 in the test group and 160 in the placebo group). Considering the dropouts, a total of 303 patients were analyzed. The test group received herbal extract and a micronutrient blend, while the placebo group received a placebo for 90 days along with lifestyle modifications. Anthropometric parameters, glycemic markers (glycated hemoglobin [HbA1c], fasting and postprandial plasma glucose, and homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance [HOMA-IR]), lipid profile, perceived stress, and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) were assessed. Results: Compared to the placebo group, the test group exhibited significant improvements in anthropometric parameters (weight, body mass index, and body fat percentage), lipid profile, glycemic control (reduced HbA1c by 6.9%, fasting plasma glucose by 15.4%, postprandial plasma glucose by 8.9%, and HOMA-IR by 19.7%), perceived stress reduction, and enhanced HRQoL (P < 0.001). The intervention was well-tolerated, with no clinically significant changes in lipid profiles, hematological parameters, or vital signs. Conclusion: Herbal extract and micronutrient blend supplementation effectively improved glycemic control, anthropometric parameters, and overall well-being in people with prediabetes, potentially reducing the risk of progression to T2DM.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: History of Diabetes: Series 1 Diabetes Care in Antiquity and Beyond: The Preinsulin Era
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Diabetes as a disease dates back to ancient times. Before the 1920s, treatment was rudimentary and largely ineffective, focusing primarily on dietary management, herbal remedies, and lifestyle modifications. Ancient civilizations, including the Egyptians, Greeks, Chinese, and Indians, recognized diabetes through symptoms such as excessive thirst and urination. They used “natural” treatments, such as dietary restrictions, physical exercise, and medicinal herbs such as fenugreek and bitter melon. Islamic scholars in the medieval period made significant advancements, recommending balanced diets and specific herbal treatments. In Europe, the preinsulin era saw the implementation of starvation diets in the early 20th century, aiming to control blood glucose by severely restricting caloric intake, though often at the cost of malnutrition. These historical approaches reflect the evolving understanding of diabetes and underscore the desperate need for effective treatments, setting the stage for the revolutionary discovery of insulin in the early 20th century.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Clinicians Perspectives of Linagliptin Monotherapy and Linagliptin + Dapagliflozin Combination Therapy in the Management of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus with Chronic Kidney Disease in Indian Settings
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Objective: The objective of the study was to gather clinician’s perspectives on the use of linagliptin monotherapy and the linagliptin + dapagliflozin fixed-dose combination (FDC) in the management of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) in the Indian clinical settings. Methodology: The cross-sectional study employed a 25-item, multiple-response questionnaire to collect expert opinions from specialists experienced in managing T2DM with CKD. The survey covered topics such as current prescribing practices, clinical observations, preferences, and experiences regarding the use of linagliptin monotherapy and linagliptin + dapagliflozin FDC in routine settings. Data analysis was conducted using descriptive statistics. Results: Overall, 1848 participants were included and the majority (77%) of them preferred linagliptin as the dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP4i) of choice, while 65% observed improved estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) with linagliptin in their practice. Nearly 44% of the respondents noted that 11%–25% of patients needed multiple drugs alongside metformin for glycemic control. Nearly 76% favored linagliptin when combined with dapagliflozin, and 61% preferred the dapagliflozin + linagliptin FDC for elderly diabetic patients with obesity or cardiac/renal issues. Approximately 68% of the clinicians reported a 3–6 mmHg reduction in blood pressure with dapagliflozin. About 60% of the clinicians stated the occurrence of urinary tract infections with the DPP4i and sodium–glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitor combination, and approximately 42% indicated effective synergy between dapagliflozin + linagliptin. Conclusion: The study findings indicated that linagliptin monotherapy and linagliptin + dapagliflozin FDC were preferred in managing T2DM with CKD due to their potency, minimal side effects, and efficacy. The study has also underscored the additional benefits conferred by linagliptin, including improved eGFR and reduced blood pressure.
